docs.title: Full Stack, End to End
docs.text:
You already know most of this.

Over the last few semesters you have studied networks, operating systems, database management, data structures and web technologies. You can define DNS. You can write a SELECT with a JOIN. You know what a process is.

What you have probably never done is watch all of it work at once, in one running program that you can break and fix.

That is what this site is for.

docs.title: What we are building
docs.text:
One project, already written, running on real infrastructure:

React + Vite runs in your browser, draws the screen FastAPI (Python) answers requests, decides what is allowed PostgreSQL (Neon) stores the data, on a server in another country

A student management system: students, courses, and the enrollments that link them. Small enough to read in an afternoon. Real enough that everything you know applies.

docs.title: Why this site is not a linear course
docs.text:
Most courses go A, B, C, D. Real software is not shaped like that. Every part touches every other part, so there is no order in which nothing is a forward reference.

Concepts is one page per idea. Never read it front to back. Look things up when you hit them, in class or in the code.

The Codebase section walks the project folder by folder, so you can start reading at any point rather than having to begin at the beginning.

You are not expected to build this from scratch

The project is finished on day one. You will read it, run it, break it, and finally extend it by adding a whole new feature yourself.

Reading working code and understanding why it is shaped that way is a bigger part of real engineering than typing new code. That is deliberate.

docs.title: The question this course exists to answer
docs.text:
By the end you should be able to answer this without hesitating:

What actually happens when you type a URL and press Enter?

You already know every piece of that answer. Right now they are stored in separate boxes labelled "Networks", "DBMS" and "Web Technologies". The job of this site is to knock the walls down.

Here is the shape of it, using the project you will be working in:

Browserlocalhost:5173 Reactfetch("/api/students") FastAPI:8000 Postgresus-east-1

Four boxes. Every one of them is something you have studied. We are going to follow that dot all the way across and all the way back, and by the end you will know what happens at each hop, what can go wrong there, and how to tell.

docs.title: JSON
docs.text:
JSON is text that looks like a Python dictionary, and it exists because a network can only carry text.

A Python dict and a JavaScript object are different things in different processes. Neither can be handed over directly. So it gets flattened to text, sent, and rebuilt on the other side.

Python dict, on the server {"name": "Aarav", "year": 2026} JS object, in the browser {name: "Aarav", year: 2026} THE NETWORK · only bytes cross this line a string of characters, nothing more {"name":"Aarav","year":2026} serialise parse FastAPI does both for you. You will never call json.dumps in this project. Because the format is just text, a Go service or a phone app joins for free.

docs.title: The entire syntax
docs.text:
Six types. That is the whole language.

{ "id": 7, "name": "Aarav", "cgpa": 8.4, "active": true,
  "graduated_on": null, "courses": ["DBMS"], "address": { "city": "Pune" } }
JSON Python JavaScript "text" str string 7 / 8.4 int / float number, one type for both true / null True / None true / null [...] / {...} list / dict Array / Object

Stricter than Python

Double quotes only. No trailing comma. No comments. And true, not True. Getting this backwards while hand-writing a curl body is the commonest cause of a 422.

docs.title: What your API sends
docs.text:
GET /api/enrollments/report, the joined view:

[ { "enrollment_id": 4, "student_name": "Aarav Sharma",
    "course_name": "Database Management Systems", "grade": "A" } ]

The database stored student_id: 1 and course_id: 3. The JSON carries names, because the JOIN happened in SQL before serialising. The browser never learns that ids exist.

Open http://localhost:8000/api/students in your browser. That tree is the exact bytes React receives.

docs.title: The error everyone hits first
docs.text:
SyntaxError: Unexpected token < in JSON at position 0

< at position 0 means you were sent HTML and tried to parse it as JSON. Wrong URL, a crash, or you forgot the /api prefix and the SPA catch-all returned index.html.

The fix is never in your parsing code. Open the Network tab and read the raw Response.

Check the status before you parse

On a 422, the body is { "detail": [...] }, not an array, so data.map(...) throws. This project checks res.ok first, in frontend/src/services/http.js.

docs.title: What JSON cannot do
docs.text:
You want JSON has What everyone does a date nothing a string, "2026-09-05" exact money only floats a string, so 0.1 + 0.2 cannot bite an image nothing a separate URL

That first row is live in your project: year is a string, so it returns as "2026".

docs.title: Status codes
docs.text:
Every response starts with a number, and the first digit tells you whose problem it is.

2xx it worked 3xx it moved, go there instead 4xx the caller was wrong. Fix the request 5xx the server was wrong. Nothing the caller does will help

4xx versus 5xx is the distinction that matters. A 4xx is the system working. A 5xx is a bug.

docs.title: Which one to return
docs.text:
Watch the three packets take three different branches.

a request arrives fields valid? row exists? allowed right now? 422 year: Field required 404 no student 99 409 still enrolled 200 / 201 201 if you created it Every branch is a check you wrote. A 500 is what happens when nobody wrote one.

docs.title: Two real bugs from this codebase
docs.text:
A missing field killed the request. POST /api/students with no year raised KeyError mid-response, so the caller got no status code at all: curl: (52) Empty reply from server. A Pydantic class now answers 422 and names the field.

A database constraint escaped as a 500. Deleting an enrolled student hit a foreign key, psycopg raised, and it surfaced as 500. That is a lie: the caller did nothing wrong and the server did not break. The request was refused for a good reason and failed to say so.

enrolled = count_enrollments_for_student(student_id)
if enrolled > 0:
    raise HTTPException(status_code=409, detail="Cannot delete " + student["name"]
        + ": still enrolled in " + str(enrolled) + " course(s).")

Why the api/ folder exists

That check cannot live in database/students.py, which only knows one table. It cannot live in React, because curl bypasses it. It belongs beside the endpoint. The folder layout is a consequence of this rule.

docs.title: The two you will keep mixing up
docs.text: 401: I do not know who you are. 403: I know exactly who you are, and no.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
curl -i http://localhost:8000/api/students/99999                     # 404
curl -i -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/students \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"name":"X"}'              # 422
curl -i -X DELETE http://localhost:8000/api/students/1               # 409

-i shows the status line. Without it you see only the body, which is how people debug a 404 for twenty minutes.

docs.title: What is an API
docs.text:
An API is a set of URLs that return data instead of a web page.

Same protocol, same server. The only difference is who the answer is for: a page is for your eyes, an API response is for another program.

Browser one request FastAPI port 8000 index.html a screen, for you JSON data, for a program GET /students /api/students The path decides which answer you get. Both come from one server.

docs.title: The rule that carries REST
docs.text:
The URL says what. The method says what to do with it.

Method URL Meaning GET /api/students all of them GET /api/students/5 just this one POST /api/students create one PUT /api/students/5 replace it DELETE /api/students/5 remove it

Never /api/getStudents or /api/deleteStudent?id=5. The URL names a thing, the method carries the action. That is why you can guess that POST /api/courses creates a course.

Open backend/api/students.py: those five functions, in that order, and nothing else.

docs.title: An API is a contract
docs.text:
Publish GET /api/students returning id, name, email, year and that shape is a promise. Rename name to full_name and every caller breaks, even though your Python still runs fine.

Safe to change Breaks your callers SQL, file names, SQLite to Postgres, adding a new field renaming a field, removing one, changing a type

We replaced the database and the whole HTTP layer in this project, and React did not change one line. That is the contract holding, and it is the reason to have one.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/students \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name":"Test","email":"t@example.com","year":"2026"}'

No browser, no React. React is only one possible caller. A phone app or a Python script would use the same endpoint.

Your live contract, generated from the code: http://localhost:8000/docs

docs.title: The problem a JOIN solves
docs.text:
Open the Enrollments page in the project. Here is what the database actually stores:

id student_id course_id enrolled_on 22 12 3 2026-09-05 23 12 4 2026-09-05 24 10 6 2026-09-05

Useless to a human. Who is student 12? What is course 3?

Now open Enrollments → See the joined report:

Student Course Teacher Fees Nisha Gupta Full Stack Web Development Mr. Kunal Mehta 5,999 Nisha Gupta Database Systems Dr. Meera Krishnan 4,499 Sanya Kapoor Computer Networks Dr. Aditi Menon 3,799

Same rows. One SQL query turned the numbers into names.

docs.title: Why the numbers are there in the first place
docs.text:
You might ask: why not just store the student's name in the enrollments table and skip all this?

**Storing the name (bad)** 
enrollments
-----------
id | student_name | course_title
22 | Nisha Gupta  | Full Stack...
23 | Nisha Gupta  | Database Sys...
**Storing the id (good)** 
enrollments
-----------
id | student_id | course_id
22 | 12         | 3
23 | 12         | 4

Now Nisha changes her email, or you spot a typo in her name.

  • Left: you must find and fix every row that repeats her name. Miss one and your data now disagrees with itself.
  • Right: you change one row in students. Every enrollment still points at id 12 and is instantly correct.

That is the whole reason relational databases exist. Store each fact once, and point at it. The pointer is called a foreign key.

docs.title: The three tables in this project
docs.text:
erDiagram
    students ||--o{ enrollments : "has many"
    courses  ||--o{ enrollments : "has many"

    students {
        int  id
        text name
        text email
        text year
    }
    courses {
        int    id
        text   title
        text   code
        text   teacher_name
        float  fees
    }
    enrollments {
        int id
        int student_id
        int course_id
    }

enrollments exists only to connect the other two. A table like that has names you will hear: join table, junction table, link table. They all mean this.

It is what lets one student take many courses and one course hold many students. That is a many-to-many relationship, and you cannot express it with two tables alone.

docs.title: The actual query
docs.text:
This is backend/database/reports.py, unedited:

SELECT
    e.id           AS enrollment_id,
    e.enrolled_on,

    s.id           AS student_id,
    s.name         AS student_name,
    s.email        AS student_email,

    c.id           AS course_id,
    c.title        AS course_title,
    c.teacher_name AS teacher_name,
    c.fees         AS fees

FROM enrollments e                          -- (1)!
JOIN students s ON s.id = e.student_id      -- (2)!
JOIN courses  c ON c.id = e.course_id       -- (3)!
ORDER BY e.id DESC
  1. Start from the join table. e is a short nickname for enrollments
  2. For each enrollment, find the student whose id matches its student_id
  3. And the course whose id matches its course_id

Read line 2 out loud as a sentence: "attach the students row where the student's id equals this enrollment's student_id." That is genuinely all JOIN ... ON means.

docs.title: What the database does with it
docs.text:
Walk one row:

  1. Take enrollment 22. It holds student_id = 12 and course_id = 3.
  2. Go to students, find id 12. That is Nisha Gupta.
  3. Go to courses, find id 3. That is Full Stack Web Development.
  4. Glue all three rows side by side into one wide row.
  5. Repeat for every enrollment.

The result is one row per enrollment, carrying columns from all three tables.

Why one query and not three

We could have fetched enrollments, then students, then courses, and matched them in Python. In fact the frontend does something like that on the Enrollments page.

But that is three trips to a database in another country, and this project measures about 2.5 seconds per trip. The JOIN is one trip, and the database is far better at matching rows than our Python loop is.

Compare database/reports.py with hooks/useEnrollments.js in the frontend. Same information, two very different approaches, and both are in this project on purpose.

docs.title: The kinds of JOIN
docs.text:
You will meet four. Only the first two matter for now.

Type Keeps Use it when JOIN (inner) only rows that match on both sides the default. You want complete pairs LEFT JOIN every row on the left, even with no match "list all students, and their courses if any" RIGHT JOIN the mirror image rare, just swap the tables instead FULL JOIN everything from both sides rarer still

Our report uses an inner JOIN, and that choice has a consequence worth noticing:

A question for class

Our report uses inner JOIN. A student who is enrolled in nothing has no rows in enrollments.

Does that student appear in the report?

No. They vanish entirely. If you wanted "every student, with a blank row when they have no courses", you would need LEFT JOIN starting from students.

Try it: edit the query, reload the Report page, see what changes.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
The best way to learn JOINs is to run them, not read them.

  • pgexercises: JOINs is real Postgres in the browser, with answers. Do these.
  • SQLBolt lessons 6 to 9 cover joins interactively.

Then come back and change the query in database/reports.py. The Report page will show your change on the next reload, and that feedback loop is the fastest way to make this stick.

docs.title: Git and GitHub
docs.text:
Git is a program on your laptop. GitHub is a website that keeps a copy.

They are separate things with confusingly similar names. Git was useful for years before GitHub existed, and you can use git all day with the wifi off.

YOUR LAPTOP git, a program. works offline your whole history GITHUB a website. needs the internet a copy, one commit behind push pull Everything happens on the left. GitHub only receives what you send it. Nothing in that box on the right is automatic.

docs.title: Which does what
docs.text:
Job Git GitHub save a version yes no see history yes shows it prettily work offline yes no back up your work no yes, this is the point let others review no yes, pull requests run tests on every push no yes, Actions

Git alone means one copy on one laptop. Lose the laptop, lose the project. That is the problem GitHub solves, and everything else it offers is a bonus.

docs.title: Four commands cover most days
docs.text:
git status                    # what have I changed?
git add .                     # mark it for the next save
git commit -m "add sorting"   # save it, locally
git push                      # send it to GitHub

status before every other command. It tells you which of the three places your work is sitting in, and almost every git confusion is being wrong about that.

docs.title: The one habit worth building now
docs.text:
Commit when something works, not when you finish for the day. A commit you can return to is worth ten you cannot describe.

This project's real history has two commits called refactor profiles controller and refactor profile controller, one letter apart. Neither tells you anything. Do better than the person who wrote those.

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
• Commits · Branches · Remotes
  • Pull requests · When it goes wrong
  • learngitbranching.js.org, the best hour you can spend on git

docs.title: Branches
docs.text:
A branch is a sticky note pointing at one commit. It is not a copy of your files.

Creating a branch writes about 40 bytes. That is why it is instant even on a huge project, and why nobody thinks twice about making one.

the split point main add-sorting Two sticky notes on one history The commits are shared up to the split. Only the notes differ.

docs.title: What the commands actually do
docs.text:
git switch -c add-sorting     # make a note here, and stand on it
git switch main               # stand on the other note
git branch                    # which notes exist, and where am I?

Switching branches changes the files in your folder to match that commit. That is the part that feels magical and is worth saying out loud: your editor's contents are a consequence of which note you are standing on.

HEAD is just "the note I am standing on".

docs.title: Why bother
docs.text:
Working straight on main Working on a branch half-finished work is the only version main always works cannot try two ideas at once one branch each, switch freely an experiment that fails must be undone delete the branch, done no review step a pull request is possible

This project's real history is entirely linear, every commit straight on main. Look at git log --oneline and you can see the cost: add 3 more CRUD pages sits between two unrelated refactors, and there is no point where you could have reviewed just one idea.

docs.title: Merging
docs.text:
git switch main
git merge add-sorting

Git takes the two photographs, works out what each side changed since the split, and combines them. If both sides changed the same lines, it cannot decide, stops, and asks you. That is a conflict, and it is normal.

Conflicts are not errors

A conflict means two humans edited the same lines. Git is refusing to guess which one is right, which is exactly what you want it to do. See when it goes wrong.

docs.title: One naming habit
docs.text:
add-student-sorting        fix-delete-500        try-postgres

Lowercase, hyphens, and name the goal, not the file you touched. fix-delete-500 still means something a month from now. asu-branch-2 does not.

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
• Commits · Remotes · Pull requests
  • learngitbranching.js.org, which exists specifically to make this picture click

docs.title: Commits
docs.text:
A commit is a photograph of every file, not a list of changes.

That surprises people. git show displays a diff, so it feels like a commit stores "what changed". It does not. It stores the whole state, and git works the difference out by comparing two photographs.

docs.title: Your work lives in three places
docs.text:
This is the model behind almost every confusing git moment.

working directory the files you edit not saved anywhere staging area what the next commit will hold still not saved repository the photographs safe. recoverable git add git commit git restore git reset Only the green box survives a mistake. git status tells you which box your work is currently in. Run it constantly.

docs.title: The hash, and why it cascades
docs.text:
688c149b2a95a5d99d8e975114fe892306666372

That is calculated from the file contents, the message, the author, the time, and the previous commit's hash. Change anything in a commit and its hash changes. Because each one contains the one before it, every later hash changes too.

That is why history is hard to rewrite quietly. It is a feature, not an annoyance.

You will normally use the short form, 688c149. Git accepts any unambiguous prefix.

docs.title: Messages
docs.text:
Useless

updatefixchangesasdfrefactor profile controller

Useful

add sorting to student tablefix 500 on deleting enrolled studentreplace SQLite with Postgres

The test: six months from now, can you find this commit without opening it? You will be reading your own messages far more often than anyone else will.

Write them in the imperative, as an instruction: add sorting, not added sorting. Git's own generated messages do this, so yours will match.

docs.title: Five commands
docs.text:
git status              # which box is my work in?
git add .               # stage everything
git commit -m "..."     # photograph it
git log --oneline       # the history, one line each
git show 688c149        # what did that commit change?

docs.title: Why committing often actually matters
docs.text:
git restore throws away uncommitted work with no undo and no warning. Nothing recovers it, because it was never saved anywhere.

Once a change is committed it is recoverable, even if you later delete the branch. That is the real argument for committing small and often: not tidiness, a safety net.

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:

docs.title: Pull requests
docs.text:
A pull request is not a git feature. It is a GitHub page wrapped around one question: may I merge this branch?

Git has no idea pull requests exist. Everything a PR does could be done with git merge on your laptop. What GitHub adds is a place to disagree before the merge happens.

branch your commits push now on GitHub pull request tests run humans comment you push fixes merged to main branch deleted review asks for a change, so you push again to the same branch The loop back is the whole point. A PR is a conversation, not a submission.

docs.title: What actually happens
docs.text:
1. Branch, commit, push. Nothing new.
  2. Open the PR on GitHub. Pick which branch merges into which.
  3. Tests run automatically. This project has .github/workflows/ci.yml, so every push gets checked.
  4. Someone reads it and leaves comments on specific lines.
  5. You push more commits to the same branch. The PR updates itself.
  6. Merge, then delete the branch.

Step 5 is the one people miss. You do not close a PR and open a new one to fix something. Push to the same branch and it appears there.

docs.title: Writing one somebody will actually read
docs.text:
Title one line, what it does. fix 500 on deleting an enrolled student Body why, not what. The diff already shows what Size small. A 40-line PR gets a real review, a 2,000-line PR gets "LGTM"

The unit is one idea

A PR that adds sorting and fixes a delete bug and renames three files cannot be reviewed, only approved. Split it.

This project's real commit Feature: add sorting, searching, export to PDF and CSV files is four ideas in one. That would have been four PRs in a professional repo.

docs.title: Reviewing
docs.text:
You will be asked to do this on your first job, probably in the first few days. Look for:

  • Does it do what the title says, and nothing else?
  • Would you understand this code in six months?
  • What happens on the unhappy path: empty input, missing row, no network?
  • Any secret, password or key in the diff?

Asking a question is a valid review. "Why 409 and not 400?" is more useful than silent approval, and it is how you learn a codebase.

docs.title: Why this exists at all
docs.text: Nobody merges straight to main on a real team, for two reasons that have nothing to do with trust: a second pair of eyes catches things, and the PR is a written record of why a change was made. Six months later, that discussion is often the only explanation anyone can find.

  • GitHub's own PR docs

docs.title: Remotes
docs.text:
origin is a nickname for a URL. Nothing more.

git remote -v
origin  git@github-bsccohort:bscCohort/pythonFullStack.git (fetch)
origin  git@github-bsccohort:bscCohort/pythonFullStack.git (push)

That is this project's real remote. origin is a habit, not a keyword. You could call it github or backup and everything would work.

docs.title: Three commands, and only one of them touches your files
docs.text: your files what you see origin/main a local note saying "GitHub was here last I looked" GitHub the actual server push · send my commits up fetch updates the note only merge changes your files git pull = fetch + merge, in one step. That is the whole difference, and it is why pull can produce a conflict but fetch never can.

docs.title: When to use which
docs.text:
Command Does Safe? git fetch updates the orange note. Touches nothing you can see always safe git pull fetch, then merge into your files can conflict git push sends your commits to GitHub rejected if GitHub moved ahead

If you are unsure what happened on GitHub, git fetch then git log origin/main --oneline. You are now informed and nothing has changed.

docs.title: The rejection you will hit
docs.text:
! [rejected]  main -> main (fetch first)

Somebody pushed while you were working, so your history and GitHub's have diverged. Pull first, then push.

Never reach for --force

git push --force overwrites what is on GitHub, including commits other people made. On a shared branch it destroys their work with no undo.

If push is rejected, git pull is almost always the answer.

docs.title: The remote is your backup, and that is the point
docs.text:
Your laptop can be stolen, dropped or wiped. A commit that has never been pushed exists in exactly one place.

Push at the end of every session, even if the work is unfinished. That is what branches are for: unfinished work on a branch harms nobody.

docs.title: When it goes wrong
docs.text:
Almost nothing in git is unrecoverable, as long as you committed.

The exception is uncommitted work. That is the whole reason to commit often.

docs.title: Start here, always
docs.text:
git status

It names your situation and usually suggests the command. Most git panic is not knowing which of the three places your work is in.

something is wrong did you commit it? yes no recoverable git reflog finds it gone forever nothing can help This single question decides everything that follows.

docs.title: The situations you will actually hit
docs.text: What happened Fix committed on the wrong branch git switch right-branch then git cherry-pick <hash> message has a typo, not pushed git commit --amend -m "better" staged a file by mistake git restore --staged file want to undo the last commit, keep the changes git reset --soft HEAD~1 pushed but GitHub rejected it git pull then push again .env got committed see below, and treat the secret as leaked lost a commit, no idea where git reflog detached HEAD git switch main

docs.title: Merge conflicts
docs.text:
Git stops and marks the file:

<<<<<<< HEAD
year = "2026"
=======
year = 2026
>>>>>>> add-sorting

Above ======= is yours, below is theirs. Delete all three marker lines and leave the code you want, which may be a mix of both.

git add the-file.py
git commit

Not an error

A conflict means two people edited the same lines and git refused to guess. It is git working correctly. Reading both sides and deciding is the job.

docs.title: A secret got committed
docs.text:
This happened in this project. backend/.env was staged, holding a real database URL and password.

Removing it from the next commit is not enough. Once it is in history, anyone who cloned the repo has it, and on a public repo it may already be indexed.

  1. Rotate the secret. Assume it is public. This is the only step that actually protects you.
  2. Add the file to .gitignore.
  3. git rm --cached backend/.env so git forgets it while your local file survives.
  4. Commit that.

Order matters. Steps 2 to 4 stop it happening again. Only step 1 fixes what already leaked.

docs.title: reflog, the actual safety net
docs.text:
git reflog

Every position HEAD has held, including commits on branches you deleted. If you committed it, it is in there, and:

git switch -c rescue <hash>

brings it back. Worth knowing before you need it.

docs.title: Two commands to be careful with
docs.text:
Command Why git push --force overwrites GitHub, including other people's commits. No undo git reset --hard throws away uncommitted work silently. No undo

Everything else in git is either safe or recoverable. These two are neither.

Not written yet

Packets, routers, IP addresses, and what your laptop actually does when it joins a network.

docs.title: The one-sentence version
docs.text: HTTPS is HTTP with the conversation encrypted, so nobody in between can read it or change it. The rules of the conversation are identical. Only the wrapper differs.

docs.title: HTTP first: it is just text
docs.text:
HTTP is a text format. That is the whole trick, and it is why you can learn it by reading it.

When your React app asks for the student list, this is what actually crosses the network:

GET /api/students HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:8000
Accept: application/json

And the answer:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 1847

[{"id":12,"name":"Nisha Gupta","email":"nisha.gupta@example.com"}]

That is it. A method, a path, some headers, a blank line, then a body. You could type it by hand, and you will, using curl.

You have already seen this by hand

Before this project used FastAPI, it read those headers itself:

length = int(handler.headers.get("Content-Length", 0))
raw = handler.rfile.read(length)

That is a program reading the Content-Length header above, then reading exactly that many bytes of body. FastAPI does it for us now, but it is the same text.

docs.title: The problem with plain HTTP
docs.text:
The text above travels through equipment you do not own: your wifi router, your ISP, a few internet exchanges, the hosting provider's network.

Every one of them can read it. And change it.

  1. You submit a login form over http://.
  2. Your password is in the request body, as plain text.
  3. Anyone on the same wifi can capture it with free software.
  4. They now have your password. You noticed nothing.

This is not theoretical. It is why browsers now mark http:// pages as Not Secure.

docs.title: What HTTPS adds
docs.text:
Three guarantees, and it is worth naming all three because people usually only know the first:

Encryption anyone watching sees scrambled bytes, not your password Integrity if someone alters the data in transit, it is detected and rejected Authentication you are really talking to bank.com, not someone pretending to be it

That third one is the one students miss. Encryption alone would be useless if you could not be sure who you had the encrypted conversation with.

docs.title: How it works, at the level you need
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser
    participant S as Server

    B->>S: Hello, I support these encryption methods
    S-->>B: Hello, pick this one. Here is my certificate.
    Note over B: Is this certificate signed by<br/>an authority I trust?
    B->>S: Agree on a secret key for this session
    Note over B,S: Everything from here is encrypted
    B->>S: GET /api/students
    S-->>B: 200 OK, [...]

The key points:

  • The certificate is the server proving its identity. It is signed by a Certificate Authority your browser already trusts.
  • The negotiation happens once per connection, then all traffic reuses the agreed key.
  • The HTTP inside is unchanged. Same methods, same headers, same status codes.

That last point matters: you do not write different code for HTTPS. Your FastAPI routes are identical either way.

docs.title: So why is this project on http://?
docs.text:
Because it is running on your own laptop, and on localhost the traffic never touches a network.

http://localhost:5173     the React app
http://localhost:8000     the API

There is no wifi router in between. There is no ISP. The data goes from a program on your machine to another program on your machine. Nobody can intercept it, so there is nothing to encrypt.

Browsers treat localhost as trusted

You will notice Chrome does not put a "Not Secure" warning on http://localhost. That is a deliberate exception, precisely because there is no network to attack.

docs.title: Where HTTPS shows up in this project
docs.text:
Two places, both worth pointing at:

1. The database connection. Look at backend/.env:

DATABASE_URL=postgresql://...neon.tech/verceldb?sslmode=require

sslmode=require is the same idea as HTTPS, applied to Postgres. Our database is in us-east-1, so that traffic crosses the real internet and absolutely must be encrypted.

2. When you deploy. Render and Vercel both give you https:// automatically, with the certificate handled for you. You will not configure it. In 2010 you would have paid for a certificate and installed it by hand; now it is free and automatic, thanks to Let's Encrypt.

docs.title: The bit that ties into CORS
docs.text:
Remember that an origin is scheme plus host plus port.

http://site.com and https://site.com are different origins. Same host, same port, different scheme. So switching a deployed app from HTTP to HTTPS can cause CORS errors that were not there before, which is a genuinely confusing afternoon if you do not know why.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
See the difference for yourself:

# plain HTTP, and you can read every byte
curl -v http://localhost:8000/api/students

# HTTPS, and you can watch the certificate exchange
curl -v https://neon.tech

In the second, look for TLS handshake, subject: and issuer: in the output. That is the certificate step from the diagram above, happening in front of you.

docs.title: Who owns what on the internet
docs.text: Almost nobody explains this part, so people end up thinking "the internet" is one thing you buy from one company. It is not. Four different companies do four different jobs, and you can change any one of them without touching the others.

docs.title: The four jobs
docs.text:
1. Registrar Namecheap, GoDaddy, Cloudflare Rents you the NAME. You never own a domain, you lease it. ₹700 to ₹1,200 / year 2. DNS host Cloudflare, Route 53 Answers "where does this name point?" Often the registrar, but need not be. usually free 3. Hosting Render, Vercel, AWS Runs your actual code on a computer that is always on. free tier, then ₹600+/mo 4. Certificate Authority Let's Encrypt Vouches that you really control this name, so browsers show the padlock. free

In this project you are already using three of them

Neon hosts the database, Render hosts the API, Vercel hosts the frontend. You have not bought a domain yet, so onrender.com and vercel.app are lending you a name on their domain. That is the only reason you have skipped jobs 1, 2 and 4 so far.

docs.title: Where the money actually goes
docs.text:
The chain is longer than most people realise:

Youpay ~₹900/yr RegistrarNamecheap RegistryVerisign runs .com ICANN~$0.20 fee
  • ICANN is the non-profit that decides which top-level domains exist at all. .com, .in, .dev are theirs to authorise.
  • A registry operates one TLD. Verisign runs .com. NIXI runs .in.
  • A registrar is a licensed reseller. This is who you actually give your card to.
  • You get a lease, renewable yearly. Stop paying and the name goes back on the market.

That is why a .com costs roughly the same everywhere: most of the price is fixed further up the chain, and the registrar competes on the small margin plus service.

docs.title: The full flow, from buying to a working site
docs.text:
1. Buy the name. You pay a registrar for mycollegeproject.com. Right now it points nowhere.
  2. Choose who answers for it. The registrar records which nameservers are authoritative. By default its own; you can point them at Cloudflare instead.
  3. Add records. In that DNS host you say "this name points at this address". See DNS records for A versus CNAME.
  4. Deploy your code. Render or Vercel runs it and gives you an address.
  5. Prove you own the name. The host asks Let's Encrypt for a certificate. Let's Encrypt checks a DNS record or a special URL to confirm you control the domain.
  6. The padlock appears. The certificate is installed automatically and https:// works.

Steps 5 and 6 used to be a paid, manual, annual chore. Let's Encrypt made them free and automatic in 2016, and it is one of the genuinely important things that happened to the web.

docs.title: What "authoritative" means
docs.text:
When you look up a name, several machines are involved, and only the last one actually knows the answer. Everyone else is caching or forwarding.

Your laptopchecks its own cache Resolveryour ISP, or 8.8.8.8 Root server"ask the .com people" TLD server"ask Cloudflare" Authoritativethe real answer

The authoritative nameserver is the one holding the records you typed in. Everyone upstream of it just points closer.

This is why a DNS change is not instant. Each layer caches the answer for a period called TTL (time to live). Set a TTL of one hour and a change can take an hour to be visible everywhere. It is not broken; it is a cache doing its job.

# See it for yourself. Ask who is authoritative for a name:
dig +short NS neon.tech

# And what the answer resolves to:
dig +short neon.tech

docs.title: SSL, TLS, HTTPS: three words, one idea
docs.text:
These get used interchangeably and it causes real confusion.

Word What it really is SSL The original protocol. Obsolete and insecure. Nobody should use it TLS Its replacement. TLS 1.2 and 1.3 are what actually runs today HTTPS HTTP carried inside TLS. The thing you see in the address bar certificate The file proving you control the name. Often called an "SSL certificate" out of habit

So when a hosting provider says "free SSL", they mean a TLS certificate, and HTTPS enabled. The word SSL survives purely because it is what people searched for in 2005.

See HTTP vs HTTPS for what TLS actually does, and Certificates and TLS for how the trust chain works.

docs.title: What you could change tomorrow, independently
docs.text:
The point of splitting the four jobs:

change registrar transfer the domain. Site keeps working, DNS records come with you change DNS host repoint nameservers. Records must be recreated at the new host change hosting deploy elsewhere, update one DNS record. Domain untouched change CA you will never do this. It is automatic

This is why "my domain is on GoDaddy but my site is on Vercel" is completely normal, and not a mistake.

docs.title: The mistake almost everyone makes once
docs.text:
Letting the domain expire. The site stops working and the failure looks like a hosting problem, because the code is fine and the server is running. Nobody can find it.

Turn on auto-renew. Put the renewal date in a calendar anyway.

docs.title: The one-sentence version
docs.text:
A web page is not allowed to read data from a different address than the one it came from, unless that other address gives permission.

That rule is called CORS: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing. It is enforced by your browser, not by the server.

docs.title: Why the rule exists at all
docs.text:
Imagine the rule did not exist.

  1. You log into your bank at mybank.com. The bank puts a cookie in your browser.
  2. In another tab, you open free-movies.example.
  3. That page runs JavaScript: fetch("https://mybank.com/api/balance").
  4. Your browser attaches your bank cookie, because the request is going to the bank.
  5. The bank sees a logged-in user and returns your balance.
  6. The movie site now has your bank balance, and you never clicked anything.

Step 6 is what CORS prevents. The request may still be sent, but the browser refuses to let the calling page read the answer.

CORS is a browser rule, not a security wall

curl has no CORS. Python has no CORS. Postman has no CORS.

# No CORS involved, this just works
curl http://localhost:8000/api/students

CORS protects users of browsers from pages they did not trust. It does not protect your server from anyone. Your server is protected by checking every request itself, which is what api/ does in this project.

docs.title: What "origin" means, precisely
docs.text:
An origin is three things joined together:

      scheme        host          port
      http://    localhost    :   5173

Change any one of the three and it is a different origin. This surprises people:

Comparison Same origin? http://localhost:5173 and http://localhost:8000 No. Different port http://localhost:5173 and https://localhost:5173 No. Different scheme http://site.com and http://api.site.com No. Different host http://localhost:5173/students and http://localhost:5173/courses Yes. Path does not count

That third row is why real apps hit this constantly, and the first row is why you hit it in this project.

docs.title: Where this bites us, exactly
docs.text:
In development we run two servers:

Reactlocalhost:5173 FastAPIlocalhost:8000

Different ports means different origins. So a fetch from the React page to the API is a cross-origin request, and the browser applies the rule.

docs.title: The two ways we deal with it
docs.text: This project uses both, for different situations. That is worth understanding, because students often assume only one exists.

docs.title: 1. In development: the Vite proxy
docs.text:
Look at frontend/vite.config.js:

server: {
  port: 5173,
  proxy: {
    "/api": {                              // (1)!
      target: "http://localhost:8000",     // (2)!
    },
  },
}
  1. Any request whose path starts with /api
  2. is quietly forwarded to the backend by Vite itself

So when React calls fetch("/api/students"), the browser thinks it is talking to localhost:5173, which is where the page came from. Same origin. No CORS involved at all.

Vite then makes the real call to port 8000 from Node, where CORS does not apply.

This is the neatest fix

The proxy makes the problem disappear rather than negotiating around it. That is why the frontend code says /api/students and never http://localhost:8000/api/students.

docs.title: 2. In production, and as a backstop: the server gives permission
docs.text:
The server can say "I allow this". In backend/main.py:

app.add_middleware(
    CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=["*"],     # (1)!
    allow_methods=["*"],
    allow_headers=["*"],
)
  1. "*" means any website may call this API

That middleware adds a header to every response:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *

The browser reads that header and decides the page is allowed to see the answer.

* is fine for a class project and wrong for a real one

allow_origins=["*"] means literally any site on the internet can call your API from a user's browser. For this course that is convenient and harmless.

In a real application you list your own site:

allow_origins=["https://myapp.com"]

If you ever also send cookies, "*" stops being allowed at all, and browsers will reject it. That is deliberate.

docs.title: The preflight, which is the part nobody explains
docs.text:
For a simple GET, the browser just sends the request and checks the response header afterwards.

But for anything that could change data, the browser asks permission first, using a different HTTP method called OPTIONS. This extra round trip is called a preflight.

sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser
    participant A as FastAPI

    Note over B: about to POST /api/students
    B->>A: OPTIONS /api/students
    A-->>B: 200, Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
    Note over B: permission granted, continue
    B->>A: POST /api/students
    A-->>B: 201 Created

So one POST from your React app can be two requests on the network. When you are watching the Network tab and see an OPTIONS you did not write, that is why.

FastAPI's CORSMiddleware answers those preflights for us. Before we adopted FastAPI, this project answered them by hand in a do_OPTIONS method.

docs.title: How to diagnose it in ten seconds
docs.text:
1. Open DevTools, Console tab. A CORS failure always says so in words.
  2. Network tab: find the request. If it is red with no status code at all, the browser blocked it before it left, or blocked you from reading the reply.
  3. Run the same URL in curl. If curl works and the browser does not, it is CORS. That single test is the whole diagnosis.
curl -i http://localhost:8000/api/students | grep -i access-control

If you see no Access-Control-* header in that output, the server is not granting permission.

docs.title: The mistake to avoid
docs.text:
Students often try to "fix" CORS in the frontend: changing the fetch, adding headers, looking for a React setting.

You cannot fix CORS from the frontend. The rule is enforced by the browser and lifted only by the server, or sidestepped by a proxy. Every real fix is on the other side.

docs.title: The Industry
docs.text:
Two questions, and they are separate.

What could I build? Web, mobile, games, cloud, data, AI and more. The differences are real but smaller than they look.

What is it actually like as a job? Which company, which rung, how much, and how you get in at all.

WHAT YOU BUILD 11 domains, 30+ titles different tools, same fundamentals you pick this early and can change it later HOW THE JOB WORKS company type rung, money, hiring nearly identical whichever path you took Every path leads into the same second box Your pay and your rung depend far more on the right box than the left. That is why these two topics live in one tab.

docs.title: The thing worth knowing early
docs.text:
A web developer and a machine learning engineer at the same company, on the same rung, are paid roughly the same. A senior engineer at a services company and a senior engineer at a product company are not, and the gap is large.

So the anxious question, "did I pick the right technology?", matters less than almost anyone tells you. The path decides what your day feels like. The company decides what your career looks like.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text: If you are wondering Read what kinds of software exist Domains of engineering what the job titles mean Roles and job titles why some companies pay double for the same work Kinds of company what "senior" actually means The career ladder what to expect in an offer Money how to get the first one How to get in

docs.title: One honest note
docs.text: Everything in this tab is a generalisation about India in 2026. Titles, ladders and numbers vary by company and go stale. Treat it as a map, not a measurement, and check levels.fyi before any negotiation.

docs.title: Kinds of company
docs.text:
The same job title pays very differently depending on who is paying. This is the single most useful thing on this page.

The reason is not generosity. It is where the money comes from.

Follow the money and the pay gap explains itself SERVICES · you are the product being sold a client your employer takes a margin you PRODUCT · the software is the product, you build it many users your employer keeps it all you, paid more In the top row your time is resold at a margin. In the bottom row your work scales without you.

docs.title: The six you will meet in India
docs.text:
Type Examples Pay What you get Services TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Accenture lowest training, structure, volume hiring Product, Indian Zoho, Freshworks, Zerodha good real ownership, sane hours Startup anything under 50 people low salary, equity breadth, speed, risk Unicorn Swiggy, Razorpay, CRED strong scale problems, good engineers Global captive Google, Microsoft, Amazon India highest depth, process, prestige Consultancy Thoughtworks, small specialists good variety, high standards

Services companies hire the most graduates by a wide margin, so most people start in the top row. That is not a mistake, it is a starting point.

docs.title: What actually differs day to day
docs.text:
Services Product Who decides what to build the client your team Codebase changes with the project the same one for years Fixing tech debt rarely funded part of the job On call for your own bugs usually not usually yes

That last row cuts both ways. Owning your mistakes in production is stressful, and it is also the fastest way to get good.

docs.title: The move that changes your pay
docs.text:
Services to product, after two or three years. You now have real experience and can clear a product-company interview, which is where the gap closes.

What clears that interview

Not your employer's name. A codebase you can explain end to end, data structures and algorithms, and being able to say why you made a decision rather than what you did.

You have the first one already. Say the words: SQLite to Postgres, and React unchanged, because the API was a contract.

docs.title: Money
docs.text:
The number in the offer letter is not the number that reaches your account. Learning to read the gap is worth more than most technical skills, and takes an afternoon.

What happens to the headline number CTC, the headline what the letter says base salary, real and monthly bonus, only if targets are met equity, vests over 4 years "benefits" padding the number arrives every month might arrive later, partly, or never Only the top row is a promise. Ask for the monthly in-hand figure. That one question cuts through everything above. A 12 LPA CTC and a 12 LPA base are very different offers.

docs.title: Rough India numbers, 2026
docs.text:
Fresher, per year, and treat these as a map rather than a measurement.

Services Product Global captive Fresher 3.5 to 5 L 8 to 15 L 18 to 30 L 3 years 6 to 9 L 18 to 30 L 35 to 55 L Senior 15 to 25 L 35 to 60 L 60 L to 1 Cr+

Read the columns, not the rows. The gap across a row is bigger than the gap down a column, which is the same point the company types page makes with the money flow.

docs.title: Equity, briefly
docs.text:
You are granted shares that vest over four years, usually 25 percent a year, often with a one-year cliff before anything at all.

Listed company shares have a price. Real money, just delayed Startup worth something only if it exits. Most do not

The trap

"12 LPA, of which 4 is equity" at an unlisted startup is an 8 LPA offer with a lottery ticket attached. Value the equity at zero when comparing, and be pleasantly surprised later.

docs.title: Three questions worth asking
docs.text:
1. What is the monthly in-hand? Cuts through CTC entirely.
  2. How much is fixed and how much is variable? Variable is a target, not a payment.
  3. What is the last appraisal cycle's average increment? Tells you the next three years.

Asking these is normal and expected. Not asking is how people end up surprised in month one.

docs.title: Negotiating, as a fresher
docs.text:
You have less leverage than later, but more than zero.

  • Never state your expectation first. Ask what the band is for the role.
  • A competing offer is the only real leverage. One other interview changes the conversation.
  • Negotiate base, not CTC. Base is what compounds into every future increment.
  • Get it in writing before you resign anything.

docs.title: Domains of engineering
docs.text:
A domain is what kind of software you work on. It is not your job title, which is a separate and messier question covered in roles.

The domains differ mainly in where the code runs, and that one fact explains most of the tooling and most of what your day feels like.

the same fundamentals loops, data, debugging grouped by where it runs Web a browser Mobile a phone Desktop their machine Cloud and infrastructure someone else's servers Data and AI a GPU, then an API Games 60 times a second Embedded and hardware a bare chip Systems and security under everything else One left box. Switching domains does not reset your career.

docs.title: All of them, side by side
docs.text:
The feedback loop column predicts your day more accurately than the language does.

Domain What you build Languages Ships as Feedback loop Web sites, dashboards, SaaS JS, Python, Java, Go a URL seconds Mobile phone apps Kotlin, Swift, Dart an app store review days Desktop installed software C#, C++, JS an installer a release cycle Cloud and infra the platform others deploy to Go, Python, YAML, Terraform a running system minutes Data pipelines, warehouses, reports Python, SQL, Scala a table others query hours AI and ML models, and things that call them Python a model plus an API hours per experiment Games games, simulation, VR C#, C++ a build seconds, then months of polish Embedded firmware for physical devices C, C++, Rust a physical device minutes, plus a cable Systems databases, compilers, kernels C, C++, Rust, Go a library or binary minutes Security breaking and defending the above Python, Go, C a report, or a fix varies wildly Quality proving it works Python, JS, Java a test suite and a verdict minutes

docs.title: The four biggest, in a bit more detail
Web
docs.text:
Where most jobs are, and what you have built. Splits three ways in practice: frontend (what people see), backend (rules and data), full stack (both). The hard part is not the code, it is the number of moving pieces in a single feature.

Start here if unsure. Not because it pays best, but because the feedback loop is shortest and the free material is best, so the transferable skills arrive fastest.

docs.title: Cloud and infrastructure
docs.text:
You build the thing other engineers deploy onto. Kubernetes, CI pipelines, Terraform, monitoring, and being the person who finds out why production is slow.

Growing fast, pays well, and hard to enter straight from college because it rewards having already operated something. Your Render and Vercel deploys are the first inch of it.

docs.title: Data and AI
docs.text:
Two related domains people conflate.

Data engineering moves data reliably from where it is created to where it is analysed. Mostly SQL and Python, and mostly unglamorous plumbing that everything else depends on.

AI and ML trains models and, more commonly now, builds products on top of models somebody else trained. That second half is much closer to backend web work than to research, and it is where most of the hiring is.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Two halves. Offensive work breaks things on purpose: penetration testing, bug bounties. Defensive work is application security, reviewing code and designing systems that fail safely.

You cannot secure a system you do not understand, so almost nobody starts here. Two or three years of building first is the normal path.

docs.title: Honest advice on choosing
docs.text:
You mostly do not have to. Every one of these hires people who arrived from web development, and the reverse is much rarer.

Two things transfer everywhere, and neither is a language:

  • Debugging, which is the actual job
  • Reading code you did not write, which is most of your first year

The trap to avoid

Picking a domain because it pays most today. Cloud paid unusually well five years ago, AI does now, and something else will next. Chasing the peak means always arriving late. Pick something you will still open on a Sunday, then get genuinely good, because seniority pays more than fashion.

docs.title: How to get in
docs.text:
Most applications are rejected by a filter that never reads your code. Understanding the funnel is how you stop taking that personally.

100 applications, honestly 100 applications sent 10 replies 6 phone screens 3 technical rounds 1 offer a filter, not a person a human at last One offer from a hundred applications is a normal, successful outcome.

The top arrow is the one that hurts and the one that is least personal. A 90 percent no-reply rate is the baseline, not a verdict on you.

docs.title: What each stage is actually testing
docs.text: Stage What it checks How to pass Resume filter keywords, degree, a link that works one page, real projects, a live URL Phone screen can you talk about your work explain your project in two minutes Technical round data structures, algorithms practice. There is no other route System design can you shape a solution usually skipped for freshers Culture round will you be pleasant to work with ask real questions

docs.title: Your project is the whole first half
docs.text:
Most graduates apply with a tutorial to-do app. You have something better, and it is worth being deliberate about saying so.

  1. Deploy it. A URL a recruiter can click beats any description of it.
  2. Write the README as if a stranger is reading. What it does, how to run it, what you would do next.
  3. Be able to explain any file. "Why is the rule in api/ and not database/?" is a question you can answer.
  4. Have three decisions ready, each with the reason.

The line that separates you from other freshers

Not "I built a full stack CRUD app". Everybody says that.

"I migrated it from SQLite to Postgres and only two files changed, because the database layer was isolated." That is a sentence about design, and juniors do not usually have one.

docs.title: Two things people skip
docs.text:
Practise data structures and algorithms. It is a filter, it is not going away, and it is learnable. An hour a day for three months clears most fresher interviews.

Apply to more places than feels reasonable. Look at the funnel again. Ten applications is not a sample.

docs.title: Rejection, briefly
docs.text:
You will be rejected far more than accepted, and mostly you will not learn why. Companies rarely give reasons.

The only useful response is to ask, once, politely, whether there is any feedback, and then keep going. The funnel is a numbers game with a skill component, and both halves need work at the same time.

docs.title: Levels and the ladder
docs.text:
As you go up, the instructions get vaguer. That is the whole ladder in one sentence.

A junior is handed a ticket that already contains the answer. A principal is handed a direction. A VP is handed a business problem.

SDE 1 · SRE 1 · Junior SDE 2 · SRE 2 SDE 3 · SRE 3 · Senior the fork · you choose here Staff Engineer Principal Engineer Distinguished / Fellow INDIVIDUAL CONTRIBUTOR Engineering Manager Director / Head of X VP Engineering / CTO MANAGEMENT Both branches are paid the same at equivalent height. Management is sideways, not up.

docs.title: The numbered part
docs.text:
Every domain numbers its early rungs the same way. SDE 1, 2, 3 and SRE 1, 2, 3 are the same ladder with a different prefix, and the same is true for Data Engineer and ML Engineer.

Rung Years What you are expected to do alone SDE / SRE 1 0 to 2 finish a well-defined ticket SDE / SRE 2 2 to 5 ship a whole feature without supervision SDE / SRE 3, Senior 5 to 8 make design decisions, unblock others, own a service

At many companies SDE 3 and Senior are the same rung, just named differently. This is also where most careers settle, and that is a perfectly good outcome.

docs.title: Above senior, individual contributor track
docs.text:
You keep going technically without managing anybody.

Rung Years The shift Staff 8 to 12 work across teams on problems nobody assigned you Senior Staff 10 to 15 not present at every company Principal 12+ set technical direction for a large area Distinguished / Fellow 15+ rare. A handful per company

The jump from Senior to Staff is the hardest on the ladder, because it is the first where doing excellent work is not enough. You have to find the work yourself.

docs.title: Above senior, management track
docs.text:
Rung Owns Still codes? Team Lead / Tech Lead a small team, often still an IC role yes Engineering Manager 5 to 10 people, their growth and delivery rarely Senior EM / Group Manager several teams, or managers no Director a department. Budget and headcount no Senior Director / Head of Engineering a large area no VP Engineering all of engineering, or a major division no CTO technical strategy for the company no

What 'Head of X' actually means

A startup title, and it maps to anywhere from Senior to VP depending on company size. "Head of Platform" at a 30-person company is often a Staff Engineer with hiring responsibility. At a 3,000-person company it is a Director.

Ask how many people report to them. That single number tells you more than the title.

docs.title: The same rung, five different names
docs.text:
Why comparing titles across companies is close to useless.

Google Amazon Microsoft Meta Typical India L3 SDE 1 SDE E3 SDE 1 / Junior L4 SDE 2 SDE 2 E4 SDE 2 L5 SDE 3 Senior E5 Senior / SDE 3 L6 Principal Principal E6 Staff L7 Senior Principal Partner E7 Principal

Ignore the word. Ask what the person is expected to decide without asking anyone. That is the only portable measure.

docs.title: Three things that are true and rarely said
docs.text:
The company gap beats the rung gap. A Senior at a services company can earn less than an SDE 2 at a global captive. Where you work matters more than how senior you are.

Switching beats waiting. Annual increments run around 8 to 12 percent. Changing company commonly means 30 to 60 percent. Not a loyalty argument, just the market.

Nobody feels senior when they get there. The title arrives before the confidence, every time.

docs.title: What to say in an interview
docs.text:
Three sentences from your own project, and each one is senior behaviour rather than junior, because each is a decision with a reason:

  • "We replaced SQLite with Postgres and only two files changed, because the database layer was isolated."
  • "Deleting an enrolled student returned a 500. It was a valid request being refused, so I made it a 409 with a message telling the caller what to do."
  • "The API is a contract. We rewrote the entire HTTP layer and React did not change."

docs.title: Roles and job titles
docs.text:
A domain is what you work on. A role is what you are called and which slice you own.

The titles are inconsistent across companies, sometimes deliberately. What follows is what they usually mean.

One system. Every role owns a slice of it. the screen React, CSS, accessibility UI / Frontend Engineer also Design Engineer the rules and the API FastAPI, validation, auth Backend Engineer / SDE both slices = Full Stack the data Postgres, pipelines, models Data / ML Engineer Data Scientist analyses it what it all runs on Kubernetes, CI, monitoring SRE / DevOps / Platform keeps it up at 3am QA Security cut across every layer One request crosses every slice. That is why roles argue about boundaries. In a startup, one person owns all four boxes and the title is just "Engineer". In a large company, each box is a separate team with its own manager.

docs.title: Building roles
docs.text:
Title What they own Also called SDE / Software Engineer the generic title. Could mean anything SWE, Developer, Programmer Frontend Engineer the screen, browser behaviour, state Client Engineer UI Engineer frontend, but closer to design. Component libraries, design systems, pixel accuracy, accessibility Design Engineer, UX Engineer Backend Engineer APIs, business rules, databases Server Engineer Full Stack Engineer both. Common in startups, rarer at scale Mobile Engineer the phone app Android / iOS Engineer Embedded Engineer firmware on a device Firmware Engineer Game Developer gameplay, engine, graphics Gameplay / Engine Programmer

UI Engineer versus Frontend Engineer

Overlapping, and the difference is real where both exist. A Frontend Engineer is judged on application architecture, state management and performance. A UI Engineer is judged on how the interface looks and feels: the design system, animation, accessibility, and whether it matches the designer's intent exactly.

If you enjoyed the Tailwind and component part of your project more than the endpoints, this is your row.

docs.title: Running roles
docs.text:
The domain where the titles are most confused, because three of them overlap heavily.

Title What they own The distinction SRE reliability as an engineering problem. Error budgets, SLOs, on call, incident response Writes software to avoid operating things by hand DevOps Engineer CI/CD pipelines, deployment, automation Often means "the person who owns the pipeline" Platform Engineer internal tooling other engineers build on Their users are colleagues, not customers Cloud Engineer AWS or GCP infrastructure, networking, cost Closer to infrastructure than to code Infrastructure Engineer servers, networks, the layer under everything Older name, still common

The honest version

At most companies these four are the same job with different words, and the title depends on who wrote the advert. The genuine distinction is SRE originated at Google as a software engineering role applied to operations, which is why SRE interviews often include the same coding rounds as SDE ones.

Read the responsibilities, never the title.

docs.title: Data and AI roles
docs.text:
Title What they own Maths needed Data Engineer pipelines, warehouses, making data trustworthy low. Mostly SQL and engineering Analytics Engineer turning raw tables into ones the business can use low Data Analyst answering questions with data, dashboards some statistics Data Scientist experiments, statistics, models that inform decisions high ML Engineer putting models into production and keeping them there medium AI Engineer building products on top of existing models, APIs, prompts, retrieval low to medium MLOps Engineer the pipeline that trains, deploys and monitors models medium Research Scientist inventing new methods. Usually requires a PhD very high

AI Engineer is the newest title here and the most accessible. It mostly means backend engineering against a model API, which is much closer to what you have already built than to research.

docs.title: Quality and security roles
docs.text: Title What they own QA Engineer testing, manual and automated SDET writing the automation. A developer whose product is the test suite Performance Engineer load testing, latency, capacity Security Engineer defending systems, reviewing designs Application Security finding and fixing vulnerabilities in code Penetration Tester breaking things with permission

docs.title: Adjacent roles you will work with daily
docs.text:
Not writing production code, and often paid comparably.

Title What they do Engineering Manager the people, not the code. See levels Product Manager decides what gets built and why Designer how it looks and how it should behave Solutions / Cloud Architect designs systems, often pre-sales Technical Writer documentation. This site is that job Developer Advocate talks and demos, half engineer half marketing Support Engineer debugs customer problems. A genuinely common route in

docs.title: How to read a job advert
docs.text:
The title is nearly meaningless. Three things are not:

  1. The responsibilities list. This is the actual job.
  2. The tech stack. Tells you what you would touch daily.
  3. Who you report to. An "SRE" reporting to IT is an operations job. Reporting to Engineering is a software job.

Two titles worth extra scrutiny

"Full Stack Engineer" at a company of eight can mean frontend, backend, deploys, database and support. Sometimes excellent for learning, sometimes just understaffing.

"DevOps Engineer" sometimes means genuine platform engineering, and sometimes means being the only person allowed to press deploy. Ask what they built last quarter.
